Water Quality
Water quality of San Jose area is good. Coyote Creek, in general, is influenced by calcium, magnesium, and bicarbonate mineral concentrations which give it the characteristic of being "hard"; however, the mineral concentrate is within the allowable levels for drinking water. Water quality in all these streams is occasionally degraded by road oils and street litter from stormwater runoff and by accidental spills from leaks in sewer lines, etc.
Groundwater resources are a significant source of fresh-water supply in the city. In the past, these resources have been drained at rates which exceeded their replenishment rate, resulting in land subsidence which has aggravated surface drainage problems. This overdraft situation has been halted by increasing the recharge rate and the subsidence problem has been at least temporarily arrested. (refer to Section II B, Geology and Soils).
The sanitary sewers in the Gardner area tend to experience infrequent exfiltration because of the age and condition of the pipelines. The exact amount of such loss is unquantifiable with present technology, but the impact on ground-water quality appears to be very minor.
Storm Drainage
Drainage in the Central and Alum Rock Planning Areas is provided by an urban storm drainage system which generally conveys run-off to one of several natural watercourses: Coyote, Los Gatos, Silver Creek, and Guadalupe River. Portions of the storm drainage system were design and installed up to 50 years ago and during the intervening years problems have developed, including the effects of subsidence. In some areas, local street flooding occurs as often as one year in three. Local storm water drainage has caused serious problems in both the Gardner and Alviso areas, hence, their inclusion in CDBG program improvements.
Drainage improvements initiated during the previous three-year CDBG program in Alviso are still underway. They include placement of storm lines in several residential streets, construction of water retention and facility to pump storm water into the slough, and placement of an earthen levee around the perimeter of the residential area of Alviso. The new CDBG funding for Alviso will accomplish the completion of the storm sewers in the streets. The other projects mentioned above are part of the earlier program.
The construction of curb ramps in the downtown area have the potential of affecting local gutter flows of storm water if improperly designed. Careful design methods should be followed in order to avoid a minor local adverse impact.
